 Advertisement Winter Outlook | Will North Carolina get snow? What Super El Niño means for snowfall and drought
 Snow may fall soon for parts of the Northeast and the Northwest, and a cooler first weekend of November will be followed by a polar push of chilly air. Still, winter is looking mild for now in North Carolina!
 Advertisement Updated: 1:03 AM EST Nov 9, 2026 Editorial Standards ⓘ Michelle Kennedy Meteorologist Winter Outlook | Will North Carolina get snow? What Super El Niño means for snowfall and drought
 Snow may fall soon for parts of the Northeast and the Northwest, and a cooler first weekend of November will be followed by a polar push of chilly air. Still, winter is looking mild for now in North Carolina!
 Updated: 1:03 AM EST Nov 9, 2026 Editorial Standards ⓘ Michelle Kennedy Meteorologist WINSTON-SALEM, N.C. — Just ask Lanie, Brian, Dave, Dylan, or me; the number one question we field this time of year is, "How much snow will we get this winter?" Currently, the 90% chance of the super El Niño continuing from fall into winter could, at worst, help improve or, at best, end drought conditions in much of North Carolina. This does not always mean good sledding snow in Winston-Salem and Greensboro. 
 Climate Outlooks for December, January and February
 Hearst Owned According to the Climate Prediction Center’s Seasonal Outlooks, North Carolina has a 30% chance of milder-than-average temperatures during the 2026-2027 winter. Hearst Owned According to the Climate Prediction Center’s Seasonal Outlooks, North Carolina’s Piedmont Triad has a 40-50% chance of above-average precipitation during the 2026-2027 winter season. This includes all kinds of precipitation, including rain, wintry mix, and snow potential. Most recent strong El Niño events and impacts in NC 
 Hearst Owned 1997 and 2015 are the most recent Decembers with a strong El Niño, or the warming of Pacific Ocean waters known to scientists as El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO) . This climate pattern has a global reach, as strong ENSO westerlies suppress tropical storm development in the summer months and interact with pressure patterns in the winter, like the Polar Vortex and North American Oscillation. In a typical ENSO event, the Piedmont Triad tends to be drier than average to the west over the Mountains and Foothills and wetter than average toward Raleigh and the coast.
 Advertisement However, a strong ENSO usually brings a few big precipitation events to the Piedmont Triad, whether it's rain, snow, or a wintry mix. In December 1997, another strong ENSO year, more than 5 inches of snow fell on the 29-30. Still, December 2015 was the fourth-wettest December on record in Greensboro at Piedmont Triad International Airport, with no snowfall reported until January 2016. This year, more heavy precipitation is possible, with NOAA's Winter Climate Outlook for precipitation running above normal, but it doesn't always correlate with higher snowfall totals.
 Hearst Owned Hearst Owned

 Average snowfall in the Piedmont Triad
 Hearst Owned 
 While colder air dipping south from the North Pole helps bring snow, it still needs to line up with the more active subtropical jet stream for several inches of snow to accumulate in the Piedmont Triad. Climate scientists and hydrologists have analyzed past events and found that moderate to strong ENSO events correlate with one to about three inches of additional snowfall for the Piedmont Triad region, and higher snowfall total anomalies are seen for the mountains, but there have been an average of 6 to 7 years with below-normal snowfall during strong ENSO years too. Forecasting snow is tricky; El Niño years also tend to bring warmer-than-average temperatures to the Carolinas. The United States Geological Survey has more on how complicated snow forecasting is during a stronger climate pattern.
 NOAA/ERA5 DATA 
The WXII 12 Weather team does not make snowfall predictions for the season; instead, we analyze the models and share the long-range forecast with viewers out to 10 days and give you the most accurate snowfall forecast a few days ahead of a winter storm. Often, it's not just about the amount of snow or rain; it's about how well we prepare you for the change in weather. Less panic and more preparation keeps us safe when driving before and after winter weather strikes.
 Hearst Owned Hearst Owned ENSO intensity is linked with changes in the Polar Vortex and other pressure patterns
 Hearst Owned When it comes to this early-season vortex collapse we're experiencing in November, or even short disruptions to the Polar Vortex, there is uncertainty about how this year's historically strong or 'super' ENSO will change local weather patterns. The Polar Vortex is just one climate system the WXII 12 First Warning Weather team will monitor as we begin the colder season.
 NASA scientist Eric Fetzer has a great video that explains the Polar Vortex and its link to the jet stream, seen here. In this video, Fetzer describes changes in the polar vortex during winter from Dec. 2013 to early Jan. 2014.
 If you love science and want to dive deeper into the connections between El Niño , the NAO and the Polar Vortex, check out a discussion here with meteorologist Adrej Flis from Severe Weather Europe .
